rationale: While peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature profiling is robustly validated for classifying KDM2B variants, the hypothesis asserting a single unified classifier achieving >95% sensitivity and specificity across overlapping chromatinopathies is challenged by several critical epigenetic nuances. Specifically, KDM2B variants do not exhibit a single homogeneous episignature; instead, loss-of-function alleles and CxxC zinc-finger missense variants produce distinct sub-episignatures. Furthermore, Levy et al. (2022) observed ambiguous or partial matches between KDM2B and other Mendelian neurodevelopmental episignatures, while Oexle et al. (2023) highlighted inherent sensitivity drop-offs for hypomorphic variants and mosaicism in standard methylation classifiers.

evidence.text: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in KDM2B generate an epigenetic signature in peripheral blood that discriminates pathogenic variants from controls. However, KDM2B episignatures bifurcate into distinct subsignatures separating loss-of-function variants from CxxC-domain missense variants, and dual molecular diagnoses complicate straightforward classification.

conflicts: KDM2B exhibits divergence into two distinct sub-episignatures (loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency vs CxxC domain missense variants), contradicting the assumption of a single uniform episignature classifier.
Partial episignature matches have been observed between KDM2B and other chromatin-modifying neurodevelopmental disorder signatures, demonstrating cross-classification ambiguity.
Standard episignature classifiers display reduced sensitivity for hypomorphic variants and somatic mosaicism, challenging strict >95% clinical sensitivity assertions across broader patient cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Does an ensemble classifier combining the KDM2B haploinsufficiency subsignature and the CxxC domain-specific subsignature improve diagnostic sensitivity for moderate-effect VUS?
new_directions.rationale: Because KDM2B variants generate bifurcated subsignatures with distinct biological mechanisms (loss-of-function vs dominant/altered DNA binding), dual-model classification could prevent misclassification of CxxC missense variants.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact pairwise classification specificity between KDM2B CxxC subsignatures and CHD7 (CHARGE syndrome) / KMT2D (Kabuki syndrome) peripheral blood episignatures?
new_directions.rationale: Direct receiver operating characteristic (ROC) benchmark comparisons on shared clinical cohorts presenting with heart, eye, and renal malformations are necessary to prove the >95% specificity claim over phenocopies.
